US Tariff Hike on Greek Automotive Exports Disrupts Sector

The US government’s decision last month to impose a 25% tariff on automotive products imported from Greece has sent shockwaves through the Greek automotive sector, with industry leaders warning of mounting losses and operational uncertainty. The measure, which came into effect on May 15, applies to a wide range of Greek-made vehicles, components, and spare parts, effectively upending trade flows that had benefited from relatively low duties.

According to provisional data released by the Hellenic Association of Automotive Manufacturers, Greek automotive exports to the US fell by 42% in value in the first two weeks following the tariff’s implementation, compared to the same period last year. “The abrupt rise in duties has made our products significantly less competitive in the American market,” said Dimitris Papadopoulos, spokesperson for the association. “Several of our members have already suspended shipments to US distributors, awaiting clarity on the duration of the measure.”

Smaller manufacturers and parts suppliers, many of whom rely on the US for as much as a third of their overseas sales, have been hit particularly hard. “Our business depends heavily on the US aftermarket for specialized components,” said Nektaria Lykou, export director at Aegean Dynamics, a mid-sized parts producer. “We are now facing difficult decisions about production volumes and staffing.”

Industry analysts warn that the sector could see longer-term consequences if the measure persists. “Greek automotive products have successfully carved out a niche in North America, particularly in the electric vehicle and specialty segments,” noted Kostas Ioannidis, a trade policy analyst at the Athens Institute for Industrial Research. “If the current situation continues, there is a real risk that US buyers will turn to alternative suppliers, possibly causing permanent loss of market share.”

In Thessaloniki, where several major automotive plants are based, union representatives expressed concern over job security. “We have already seen temporary layoffs at some facilities,” said Yannis Christidis of the Federation of Automotive Workers. “If exports do not recover soon, the impact on employment could be severe.”

The Greek government has stated it is seeking to resolve the dispute through diplomatic channels but, as of this week, the US tariffs remain in place and the sector faces ongoing uncertainty.
